### 4.3.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Faced with the destructive reality of covert *bedrog* and the bad-faith design of *persuasive AI*, traditional civil law doctrines must be radically reconstructed to prevent them from losing their relevance (Hildebrandt, 2015; Brownsword, 2020). Under the framework of Indonesian positive law, particularly Article 1320 in conjunction with Article 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek), an agreement is declared null and void or voidable if the consent given suffers from a defect caused by mistake (*dwaling*), duress (*dwang*), or fraud (*bedrog*) (Subekti, 2005; Pitlo, 1978). A novel doctrinal construction must expand the interpretation of fraudulent artifices (*listige kunstgrepen*) to encompass the concealment of artificial agency, the engineering of algorithmic latent spaces, and affective manipulation perpetrated by artificial intelligence systems (Calo, 2014; Rasetto, 2021). If a system provider intentionally designs an interface that obscures non-human identity in order to induce a legal subject to enter into a contractual obligation, such an act must legally be qualified as covert fraud that invalidates the consent given (Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code).

Furthermore, the doctrine of undue influence or abuse of circumstances (*gebrekkige toestemming*), which has hitherto been applied primarily within traditional power dynamics such as those between doctor and patient or lawyer and client, must be integrated into the relationship between humans and *persuasive AI* entities (Bigwood, 2003; Van Dunné, 2015). When a system's computational architecture succeeds in generating a psychological dependency that paralyzes the subject's autonomy of will, any digital contract, transaction, or consent resulting from such a condition must be deemed legally vitiated because it stems from a situation exploiting cognitive vulnerability (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008; Farahany, 2023). In this context, civil liability must not be shifted onto the victimized user; rather, it must be attributed upward to the developers, platform providers, and corporations that design, train, and distribute these bad-faith *persuasive AI* systems (Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code; Wiethoff, 2021).

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in the digital era also demands the harmonization of private law doctrines with progressive personal data protection instruments—such as the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022)—as well as global standards like the *EU Artificial Intelligence Act* (Regulation 2024/1689). The right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, must be elevated to a fundamental pillar within the doctrine of contractual validity (Hildebrandt, 2015; Lynskey, 2019). 

The mathematical-philosophical model of consensus validity can be formulated as follows:

$$ \text{Contractual Validity} = f(\text{Cognitive Autonomy}) - \left( \sum \text{Latent Space Manipulation} + \text{Illusion of Artificial Intimacy} \right) $$

If the value yielded by this function demonstrates that a consensus arises from cognitive distortion intentionally induced by a machine, civil law must provide an effective remedial mechanism in the form of full damages and immediate contractual rescission (*restitutio in integrum*) (Asser, 2004; Subekti, 2005).

In conclusion to this discourse, 21st-century civil law jurists face a historical summons to rescue the meaning of human autonomy from the clutches of surveillance capitalism and algorithmic manipulation (Zuboff, 2019; Susskind, 2020). The law must not remain passive, hiding behind obsolete dogmatic formalism while persuasive algorithms continually erode the foundations of free will that animate the private law system (Brownsword, 2020). By reforming the doctrines of *bedrog* and undue influence, and by upholding the principle of substantive justice above the illusion of digital consensus, we not only rescue individual victims from the snares of the digital wolf in sheep's clothing, but we also restore moral integrity and human dignity to the very heart of the modern civil law system (Jonas, 1979; Habermas, 1981).
